headline: Vermont UniFirst settlement ends automatic renewals and orders customer refunds
dek: The company will stop using automatic-renewal language in Vermont contracts, notify customers and pay the state $60,000 after an attorney general investigation.
body: Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark announced an agreement with UniFirst on Oct. 14 that will change how the uniform and facility-services company handles long-term contracts in the state. Under the settlement, UniFirst will stop including automatic-renewal language in its Vermont contracts, send customers notice of the change and pay the state $60,000. The [Vermont Attorney General’s Office announcement](https://ago.vermont.gov/blog/2026/10/14/attorney-general-clark-enforces-vermonts-automatic-renewal-law) said the agreement resolves an investigation into whether UniFirst complied with Vermont’s automatic-renewal law.

The settlement also addresses customers who were charged for ending a contract early during the period when the company was out of compliance. Those businesses are to receive refunds, although the attorney general’s announcement does not state how many customers are affected or give a total dollar value for the refunds. The $60,000 payment to Vermont is therefore separate from the money that may go back to customers. The office said people who believe they were affected can contact its Consumer Assistance Program by calling 800-649-2424 or emailing AGO.CAP@vermont.gov.

The dispute matters because automatic renewal clauses can turn a routine service agreement into a continuing obligation unless a customer spots the term and cancels on time. UniFirst supplies workplace uniforms, protective clothing and facility services, so the contracts at issue can involve recurring services rather than a one-time retail purchase. Vermont Business Magazine, which published an account of the settlement, reported that the company will abandon automatic contract renewals in Vermont and that businesses charged early-termination fees during the noncompliant period will be refunded. The settlement does not say that every current UniFirst customer will receive money; the refund provision is tied to the period and charges described by the state.

Vermont’s statute sets several conditions for an automatic renewal involving a consumer contract with an initial term of at least one year and a subsequent renewal longer than one month. The contract must describe the renewal clearly and conspicuously in plain language and bold type, and the consumer must take an affirmative step to opt in. If the customer opts in, the seller must provide written or electronic notice between 30 and 60 days before the earliest of the renewal date, termination date or cancellation deadline. The notice must identify the termination date and the length and additional terms of the renewal. The [Vermont General Assembly’s statutory text](https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/09/063/02454a) also requires an accessible cancellation method, including an online option when the contract was accepted online.

The law gives the attorney general’s action a broader consumer-protection context, even though the UniFirst announcement specifically discusses Vermont businesses. A company that rents uniforms or provides facility products may serve a restaurant, manufacturer, health-care operation or public-facing workplace, and the cost of an unwanted renewal can accumulate through service charges or an early-termination fee. That is why the practical question for a customer is not simply whether a contract contains renewal language, but whether the customer received the disclosures and cancellation opportunity the law requires. The settlement changes UniFirst’s contract practice; it does not remove the statute’s requirements for other sellers or service providers.

The agreement also leaves important details for follow-up. The attorney general’s release does not identify the number of Vermont customers who may qualify for refunds, the average amount of any charge or the date by which all notices will be delivered. It likewise does not describe an independent finding by a court; this is an enforcement settlement announced by the attorney general’s office. Businesses reviewing old UniFirst agreements should preserve contracts, renewal notices, invoices and records of any early-termination charge before contacting the state, because those documents may help establish whether a particular account falls within the settlement’s terms.

For Vermont customers, the immediate next steps are notice and review. UniFirst is expected to tell customers that the automatic-renewal language will no longer appear in its contracts, and eligible businesses should watch for information about refunds rather than assume that the state payment covers them directly. The Consumer Assistance Program can explain how to raise an individual concern. The state’s action is a reminder that renewal terms are enforceable business practices with real costs, and that the deadline to cancel a service agreement should be treated as carefully as the price and scope of the service itself.

seoTitle: Vermont UniFirst settlement ends automatic contract renewals
seoDescription: Vermont’s attorney general says UniFirst will stop automatic-renewal language, notify customers, refund certain charges and pay the state $60,000.
